summary: Specifies the lock function for MPLS Transport Profile networks, which lets an operator stop a path carrying client traffic while keeping test and OAM traffic going. It also describes how loopback works, so a node returns what it receives. It updates RFC 6371.

plainLanguage.summary: Before fixing a road, workers close it to normal cars but let test vehicles through. This defines the same idea for network paths, plus a mode where a node sends everything back.

questions: how to take a transport path out of service
what is the mpls loopback function
how to lock an mpls transport path
subtitle: How MPLS-TP operators take a transport path out of service for maintenance, and test it with loopback.

tldr.problem: Operators of MPLS transport networks need to stop a path from carrying client traffic, for maintenance or testing, in a coordinated way at both ends.
tldr.mechanism: A management Lock command takes the path out of service at each end, and an optional Lock Instruct (LI) OAM message, sent periodically, helps the two ends lock together. Loopback, done by management commands, then lets a node return all received data for testing.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the LI message and its ACH Type 0x0026, and updates Sections 7.1.1 and 7.1.2 of RFC 6371 so LI needs no response.

today: RFC 6435 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2011. It updates RFC 6371, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Lock and Loopback
sections.content:
Two useful Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) functions in a transport network are lock and loopback. Lock lets an operator stop a transport path from carrying client traffic. Test traffic and OAM messages can still be mapped onto it. It may apply to Label Switched Paths (LSPs), Pseudowires (PWs), including multi-segment Pseudowires, and bidirectional MPLS Sections.

Loopback lets an operator set a specific node on the path into loopback mode, so it returns all received data. It tests the integrity of the path to and from that node. It requires that the path be locked, and that a Maintenance Entity Group End Point (MEP) send test data and check it on receipt.

The RFC specifies the lock function for MPLS and describes how loopback operates.
sections.plainLanguage: Lock closes a road to everyday traffic. Loopback makes a spot on the road turn test cars around so you can see if the road works.

sections.title: What It Changes in RFC 6371
sections.content:
This document updates Sections 7.1.1 and 7.1.2 of RFC 6371. That framework assumed the Lock Instruct message independently enables locking and requires a response message.

The mechanism here requires management to send the lock instruction to both ends of the path, and the Lock Instruct message then does not require a response.
sections.plainLanguage: The old plan had one end ask and wait for an answer. Now both ends are told directly, so no answer is needed.

sections.title: The Lock Function
sections.content:
Lock asks a MEP to take a transport path out of service for administrative reasons, such as maintenance. The NMS or a management process sends a Lock command, and the MEP stops injecting or forwarding traffic onto the path. Both directions must be taken out of service, so the command goes to the MEPs at both ends. That means lock can be done entirely in the management plane.

Coordinating two management messages tightly can be hard on a busy management plane. To help, a MEP can also send a Lock Instruct (LI) OAM message. A MEP locks a path when it gets a management command or when it receives an LI message.

The LI message is based on a new ACH Type and an existing TLV. It works for LSPs, PWs and bidirectional MPLS Sections.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends of the road must be closed or cars still sneak in from one side. A quick signal between the ends helps them close at the same moment.

sections.title: The Lock Instruct Message
sections.content:
The LI message travels in the Generic ACH and is identified by a new PW ACH Type of 0x0026. Its fields are:

  • Version: currently 1.
  • Reserved: MUST be zero on transmission and SHOULD be ignored on receipt.
  • Refresh Timer: the maximum time between successive LI messages, in seconds. The default is 1 and 0 is not permitted. It MUST NOT change during a lock, and a receiver MAY ignore a changed value.
  • MEP Source ID TLV: one of the three MEP Source ID TLVs defined in RFC 6428, identifying the MEP that sent the message.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is a short card saying who is closing the road and how often they will repeat the announcement.

sections.title: Locking and Unlocking
sections.content:
A MEP that gets a management Lock command MUST take the path out of service. For rapid coordination, it MUST then send LI messages to the MEP at the other end, setting the Refresh Timer and retransmitting at that rate. A MEP may see the command or an LI message first, and MUST take the path out of service immediately in either case. It is locked if management requested it or it is receiving LI messages.

A receiving MEP identifies the path from the label stack. An LI message is in error if there is no matching label binding, or if the Source MEP-ID is unexpected for the MEG. With no return path, such as a unidirectional path, the MEP cannot lock the return direction. A MEP MUST NOT apply a lock for an errored message; it SHOULD perform local diagnostics such as counting, and MAY log them.

On an Unlock command a MEP MUST cease sending LI messages, but stays out of service while it still receives them. So management must send Unlock to both ends. A MEP that is unlocked and has not received an LI message for 3.5 times the Refresh Timer, or never did, puts the path back into service.
sections.plainLanguage: Each end keeps the road closed as long as someone ordered it or the other end keeps announcing it. Reopening needs both ends released and a short quiet wait.

sections.title: The Loopback Function
sections.content:
Loopback is done through management commands, so no protocol is specified. The target node is set into loopback mode, a MEP sends a pattern of test data, and the node loops everything back so the MEP can compare. A forwarding plane loop is configured so the incoming direction is cross-connected to the reverse direction. Data-plane loopback is an out-of-service function that loops back all traffic, including user data and OAM, unmodified except for normal per-hop processing such as TTL decrement. For an intermediate point it is configured on the ingress or egress interface through management.

Prerequisites:

  • The path must be bidirectional, so there is a return path.
  • The node must be on both forward and return paths. This holds for all MEPs and MIPs on a co-routed bidirectional LSP, a PW or a bidirectional Section, but only for MEPs on associated bidirectional LSPs.
  • The path must be locked first, and management must ensure both MEPs are locked before setting loopback.
  • The MEP must not send test data until loopback is configured.
  • Test packet TTL must be large enough for both directions.
  • OAM messages cannot reach points beyond the loopback node until loopback is lifted.

Measuring packet loss, delay and delay variation with loopback traffic is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A mirror at the far end of a hallway sends your shout back, but only if the hallway is closed to others first and your shout is loud enough to make the round trip.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
MPLS-TP is a subset of MPLS and builds on its security model, which assumes it is very hard to inject traffic into the network. The protocol is carried in the G-ACh, so it depends on that channel's security, as described in RFC 5586 and RFC 4385.

The G-ACh can be used as a covert channel. That is wider than this document, but the channel provides end-to-end connectivity and SHOULD NOT be policed by transit nodes. Because the G-ACh is essentially connection-oriented, injecting or modifying these control messages requires subverting a transit node, which is considered hard and impossible to protect against at the protocol level. Management-level techniques are more appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages ride a private lane, so a sneak would have to take over a stop along the way. Guarding the stops is a job for network managers.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: LI OAM needs a unique Associated Channel Type. IANA assigned value 0x0026, description LI, in the "Pseudowire Associated Channel Types" registry, with no TLV following in the registry's "TLV Follows" column, referencing RFC 6435.
sections.plainLanguage: The Lock Instruct message got its own official ID number so nobody mixes it up with other messages.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero on transmission, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Refresh Timer
fields.desc: Maximum seconds between LI messages; default 1, 0 not permitted.

fields.name: MEP Source ID TLV
fields.desc: Identifies the MEP that originated the message (variable length).
